utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom today. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have appearances for the day starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honour. Ms. Ann Sutherland and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution, together with myself, Dan Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Novak Lukic; Daniela Tasic, our case manager; Chad Mair; Tina Drolec; Eadaoin O'Brien, one of our interns; and my name is Gregor Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the record reflect that we're sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis today because for reasons unavoidable Judge David is not with us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I remind you you're still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I first want to take you back to something that you said at the very beginning of the hearing last Thursday which appears at transcript pages 1043 and 1044. You were making corrections to events which occurred in the Republic of Serbian Krajina in early 1991. You mentioned three dates. On the transcript page 1043 at line 23, you mention the 28th of February, 1992. On transcript page 1044, line 1, you mentioned the 1st of April, 1992, and on line 3 of the same page you mention the 25th of April, 1992. Now, the 25th of April, 1992, date was corrected by you to 1991. However, the two dates you also mentioned before that were not picked up. For the correctness of the record with the remaining two dates, that is the 28th of February, 1992 and the 1st of April, 1992, did you, in fact, mean to say 1991 and not 1992?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In relation to the correctness of the record, are there any other matters that you wish to draw the attention of the parties in the court to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What are they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very end of the session on Thursday, there was some discussion of the phrase "strategic goals," and I compared the two phrases -- or that phrase as it appeared in two different documents. I believe I said that they were the same in Serbian. In fact, there is a slight difference between the two phrases in Serbian as they appeared in those two documents that the difference being in the first word of the phrase, the word that was rendered in both cases in English as "strategic." The adjective in Serbian in the two different cases takes a slightly different form. The second word of the phrase "goals" is the same. That word was translated in two different ways in those two different documents. So there is a slight difference between the two phrases as they appeared in those documents in the first word of the phrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Perhaps then we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. I appreciate the correction, but I'm not sure I understand precisely what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Neither do I.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, it might assist if we can quickly go -- turn back to those two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, the two documents you were referring to were the last two documents that you were shown, that is P193.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If that could be brought up onto the screen, please. And I think that is at pages 41 to 42 of the English translation and pages 49 to 51 of the B/C/S. And if we could go to the bottom of page 42 where Dobrica Cosic is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that the -- is that the paragraph you were referring to, Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Actually, I believe the document I was referring to was the last document in the session, which I think is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 194.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the other document was the 16th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In relation to P194, if we could go to page 127 of the English translation and page 137 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's me alone, but on this English channel I keep hearing some people way in the background. Are there crossed lines somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mean the ghosts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, there are ghosts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At least we're all hearing them. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Treanor, you were talking about point 9 of -- of Zivota Panic's discussion?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I think I can make the point just looking at this particular document. We discussed point nine where it says "strategic aims." The word aims is the word that had been translated before as goals. That word is the same as we had seen it in the 16th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. The first word which here is translated as "strategic" in Serbian is slightly different than the Serbian adjective that we saw before in the 16th session. Here the adjectival form is used is strategiski as opposed to strateski in the 16th session. So there is that difference between the two adjectives. They're both formed from the same root, however.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Chamber the differences as you see them between the two?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that the meaning of the two words is the same. They've been translated the same in English. One could perhaps capture the difference by saying strategic and strategical. I think those two words exist in English. I'm not aware if they have any difference in meaning either. I just wanted to point out that minor difference in the two phrases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Treanor. I want to assume that Mr. Guy-Smith doesn't know B/C/S and that his objection, I thought, was based on the substitution of the word "goals" with the word "objectives." I'm not quite sure whether he understood -- he was -- I'm not quite sure he was objecting to the word "strategic," but he's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right. That was my objection at the time. I'm pleased to receive the education with regards to the difference between the adjectival use of strategic, which is a different matter. Whether strategic and strategical mean the same thing is something perhaps that we can take up at a different point, but Your Honour is right. That was what my concern was at the time, but apparently we remain in the same state of play as regards to that particular issue, I gather, from what Mr. Treanor has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, was there anything else?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As everyone is aware during last Thursday's hearing, there were a number of technical glitches with the documents in e-court. I would have liked to have dealt with those documents before we moved on today, but unfortunately I'm unable to do so until they're uploaded into e-court, which hasn't yet occurred. However, one of the exhibits which was MFI'd, that's P184, I wish to tender the pages that were identified during Thursday's hearing. P194 MFI was first called up at transcript page 1079, line 17?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. Are you talking about P184 MFI, because 194 was not MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: P184. I'm sorry, Your Honour. It was first called up as 65 ter number 06668. The exhibit was MFIed at transcript page 1088. The registrar and case manager located the pages which had been discussed by Mr. Treanor, which were subsequently read into the record by the registrar at transcript page 1107. I now wish to tender those pages as Exhibit P184.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those pages are admitted into evidence as Exhibit P184.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The Defence queried the source of two exhibits at transcript pages 1132 in relation to P194 and transcript pages 1139 in relation to P194. In addition, the Defence queried whether the OTP was in possession of audios of both of these exhibits. Inquiries have been made with respect to the two queries, and regarding the source, I said at transcript page 1132 that it was provided by the Serbian government; however, at that time it was known as the federal republic of Yugoslavia, i.e., the government of the Republic of Serbia and Montenegro. With regard to the query re: The audio, the FRY government did not provide the OTP with audios of either of these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The transcript refers to one exhibit, Madam Sutherland. I know that you did mention exhibits twice, but I also heard you mention P194 twice instead of two separate exhibits. Just look at page 7, line 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, on page 6 -- or for me it's page 6, line 25, but obviously on your screen it's page 7, line 1, the first exhibit that I mentioned was P193.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see. I don't have page 25 at page -- I mean, line 25 at page 6, unfortunately. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I mentioned two exhibits, P193 and 194.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the -- the page number is also incorrect on that first page. It's transcript page 1132.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Instead of?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't appear in the transcript. P193 was discussed at transcript page 1132 and P194, the query was raised at transcript page 1139.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, on Thursday afternoon, Mr. Treanor, we had been dealing with the documents in relation to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and if we can turn back to that topic now. You mentioned earlier in your testimony that Dobrica Cosic was the president of the FRY. Who became president after Dobrica Cosic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Lilic was the next president of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When was he elected to that position?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have Rule 65 ter number 06824. Page 1 -- it's a one-page document, both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can see from this document, that occurred on the 25th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who appointed him. Who -- who passed that decision, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was elected by the Federal Assembly of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was the chief of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavian army when Lilic became president?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If by "chief" you mean the chief of staff, the chief of staff at that time was General Zivota Panic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who did Lilic subsequently appoint as chief of the General Staff of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who did Lilic subsequently appoint as Chief of the General Staff of the army of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lilic shortly thereafter appointed General Momcilo Perisic as Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 05046 on the screen, please. Page 1 of each of the B/C/S and English at the moment and then onto page 2 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did this occur, Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That occurred on the 26th of August, 1993. As can be seen in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can those -- that document and the previous document, so Rule 65 ter number 06824, may that be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say 6824, 06824 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That was the decision on the election of Lilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. 65 ter 06824 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P195, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And 05046 is also admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P196.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to now direct your attention to legislation that was passed by the FRY Assembly in relation to the army. Can you tell the Court what -- what law was passed and when?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I have Rule 65 ter number 00426 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two major pieces of legislation came into effect at the end of 1993, a Law on Defence and a law on the army of Yugoslavia. They came into effect provisionally in October 1993, and they're -- and they came into effect in their final form in May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Turning to the law on the army, does this govern the duties and responsibilities of army personnel including the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could take you to Article 4 of the -- the law on the army, which is on page 2 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the -- sorry, page 1 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English translation. Who commands the army in -- under -- under this legislation?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in terms of Article 4, as we can see in the first paragraph it states "The president of the republic shall command the army in war and peace in accordance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, may this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P197, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, we've dealt with the Serb political entities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Croatia, the Republic of Serbia in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I want to turn now to discuss international developments which affected these Serbian entities and the relations among -- amongst them. I would like to take you back to April 1992. Towards the end of April what position did the FRY take vis-a-vis the other republics of the -- what were then SFRY?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It adopted a --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I could -- could correct myself. At that time they were no longer republics of the SFRY, but I meant in relation to republics of the former SFRY. If I could have 65 ter number 06695 on the screen, please. Page 1 of the B/C/S and English and then onto page 2 of the English translation. I'm sorry, I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On 27 April 1992, representatives of the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro adopted a declaration which dealt with those relations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And basically what was the position?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would call the Court's attention to paragraph numbered 4 in that connection, which is on the next page of the English translation. Paragraph 4 in the middle of the page. "The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has no territorial pretensions against any of its neighbours. Respecting the aims and principles of the United Nations charter. The CSCE documents it shall adhere strictly to the principle of using non-violent means to resolve any open issues." The CSCE is the abbreviation for the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe, which later on became known as the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, from documents that you've reviewed and some of which we will see subsequently, was that, in fact, the case, that FRY had no territorial pretensions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. I -- before the witness answers the question, I think it's outside the purview of his expertise, and it calls for a legal conclusion with regard to relatively critical issue. If the witness wishes to, through examination, point to documents it's different than drawing the conclusion at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my submission Mr. Treanor can answer this question. He has reviewed numerous documents, and he can give his opinion based on his review of those documents as to whether, in fact, this statement is -- is a correct one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you doubt the correctness of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why? Why do you doubt it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I don't want to give evidence from the bar table, Your Honour, but we will see clearly from documents that will be coming up that they were -- the FRY were clearly involved in the territory of the former republics of the SFRY -- the republics of the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The problem is this witness is not a fact witness. Now you want him to confirm a fact. He's an expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you're saying to me that other documents are going to come and contradict this document, then let so be it. Then the question is he the person who can reconcile any contradictions or not, and if he is, then you can ask him so, but I'm not quite sure whether he's here as a fact witness. If you're asking him to confirm a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm asking him to give me an opinion in relation to all the documents that he has reviewed whether, in fact, that statement as -- as it stands, as it reads, is correct. We can move on, Your Honour, and we can demonstrate through the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what implications did this declaration that you have -- I'm sorry, could that document be admitted into evidence, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You haven't given us the 65 ter number. What is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 06695. I thought I brought the document up onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 06695. Oh, sorry. I probably didn't take it down. Thank you very much. The exhibit is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P198, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what implications did this document have for the FRY and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if I could have 65 ter number 06693 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the date that declaration was adopted, the JNA was still present in BH, and shortly thereafter the FRY -- the new FRY authorities agreed to withdraw the JNA from BH by a certain date. I believe the date was the 19th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can take you to page 4 of the English translation and page 4 of the B/C/S. Mr. Treanor, this is minutes of the 197th session of the Presidency of the SFRY. What did they agree in relation to the JNA at this session?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this session of the Presidency of the SFRY, which if I can remind the Court was exercising the powers of the president of the new FRY pending the election of the president, the Presidency of the SFRY made certain decisions about the -- the -- the Yugoslav army as it was now called in relation to its presence in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did they decide?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would call the Court's attention to the English under Item 2, which is item 2 in the agenda. I won't read the whole thing certainly. In the second paragraph under that item, the Presidency calls for members of the JNA in BH to return to Yugoslavia within 15 days at the latest, and in the second paragraph, if I could read that, there was -- there's a slight problem perhaps in the translation. "Given that this process will be concluded within 15 days at the latest, the Yugoslav Presidency has estimated," not "decided," "that according to the SFRY constitution, there are no grounds for the Yugoslav Presidency, or any other Yugoslav organ, to make decisions regarding military issues on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And the next paragraph I would just read a bit because again there appear to be a couple of translation issues. "The Yugoslav Presidency has concluded," not "decided," "to call on the leaderships of all three national," "national," not "ethnic," "communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, to reach an agreement and make a decision on taking on the JNA which is made up of citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to avoid unwanted situations and consequences." The army was still at this point officially known as the JNA of the new name. The new name, Yugoslav Army, was not officially adopted until the 19th or the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I note in your -- in your reading, Mr. Treanor, that you're skipping what is written in the English translation as "that part of the JNA."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. Those words do not appear in the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So just a second. I'm trying to understand this document as translated by Mr. Treanor. So do I understand you to be saying, then, that the JNA that is made up of citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina will stay in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it -- first a decision being made. That would be part of the decision, I imagine. It doesn't say that they would necessarily stay there pursuant to that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My understanding of your translation was that the Presidency has concluded, not decided, to call on the leadership of all three national communities, Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, to reach an agreement and make a decision on taking the JNA, which is made up of citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the decision that is anticipated from these national communities is that they must take up the JNA that is made up of those citizens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. In other words, members of the JNA that are citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I agree that the words -- that "part of" would logically fit in that sentence, but, unfortunately, they're not in the original, but that would be the sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I thank you. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear, just with regard to what the witness just said, because as we understand the issue of translation and interpretation is, in fact, an art and not a science. Since he indicated that that particular language "that part of the JNA" makes sense. Do I understand what the witness is saying those words are not contained in the document, but the document itself would give that as a meaning? I'm just unclear as to what he's saying at this point in particular, whether he's discussing a literal -- whether it's literally written a particular way, Your Honour or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, as I understand him yes the words are not mentioned in the original, but that interpretation would be the logical interpretation because some of the members of the JNA will not necessarily be citizens of BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to make sure because I don't want to dwell on points that don't need to be dwelt on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. But be that as it may, this now -- may I ask a question. Is this an official translation or is this a draft translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: One moment. It's a draft official translation, Your Honour, draft CLSS translation. Official being what you termed the other day as the CLSS unit that has -- that was set up. So this is a draft of -- from the CLSS. I was going to ask Your Honour to mark it for identification and then we would seek to get a revised translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Sutherland. It is with that in mind that I was asking the question. Then 65 ter 06693 will be made -- may it please be given an exhibit number and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P199 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 02144.01 on the screen, please, at page 353 of the English translation and 422 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess -- if I may just sound a warning. We are going to do admit only the pages you deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are dealing with so many --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That said, the previous document 6693 is a five-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So that document is admitted in its entirety, whereas the next document is quite substantive.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, so how did the withdrawal of the JNA work out, in fact?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of the next document, we're going to be seeing, the JNA officers and men who were in Bosnia and were citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina that remained there and became part of the Bosnian Serb forces. Also, a bunch of its equipment was left there and was taken over by the Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This document that is on the screen is -- is it not a transcript of a continuation of the 34th session of the SDS Assembly on the -- held on the 28th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. In fact, that was a very long session extended over several days in the course of over a month. This particular statement was made on the 11th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I took you and the Court to page 353 of the English translation and 422 of the B/C/S in order so that they could see the speaker. Who is speaking at this session?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milan Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then if I could go to page 354 and 423 of the English and B/C/S respectively. Can you tell the Court General Gvero's position in August 1993 reflecting back on -- on the withdrawal of the JNA in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I could call the Court's attention to the first full paragraph in the English translation beginning with "The SDS --" I'll just read that paragraph and the following sentence and the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That whole long paragraph do you want to read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No that particular paragraph beginning with the SDS is -- it's five lines long mercifully. If I could read that in the first sentence of the next paragraph. General Gvero says: "The SDS and the state institutions that have established -- that have been established take the most credits for arming the Serb people with personal weapons, which was made possible by the rapid support of the many Serb officers in the commands of the former JNA on the territory of the former BH, Serbs in internal affairs institutions, if you will, and in the political institutions of the army and Serbia, that is the FRY." And the beginning of the next paragraph: "In May 1992, after the JNA left our territory, the army of Republic of Srpska was established, and Serbs from the former JNA were appointed to the most important commanding positions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I note once again that your translation is not identical with the translation as we have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. There were a couple --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once again I ask the status of this translation. Is it an official translation? Is it -- is it and final translation? Is it a draft translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's a draft -- draft translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does General Gvero also talk about the -- the weapons to be left -- that were left there? Does he --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he makes -- he makes a statement addressing the equipment of the Bosnian Serb forces. Further down in that paragraph, there's just one sentence I would draw the Court's attention to. It's at the very bottom of the English as appearing on the screen now. The line beginning with "No one to ask," the first full sentence begins: "We had neither a budget to support us nor the material resources to fight the war. Not a single plane or helicopter has been bought, nor any artillery weapons, et cetera."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, if I can just take you back up to the paragraph beginning "In May 1992," and towards the end of that paragraph, does General Gvero say anything about the direction -- the direction of the -- the -- that would be taken?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He says -- in referring to -- referring to the main tasks of the army: "All the human and material resources were kept that could help improve the situation on the front. The principle direction was establishing a combat force and keeping the unity of all the Serb people in order to achieve the goals of war."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that page may be admitted into evidence and marked for identification while we get a revised translation of that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Only that page or also 353?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I simply took you to page 353 so that you could see where Gvero was starting the conversation so you that knew who the person -- the speaker was, but the page -- the only page that I'm interested in or we're interested in is page 354 of the English translation and 423 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Page 354 of 65 ter 02144 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P200 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes. Thank you so much. Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, in light of what we've just seen, what position did the international community take in relation to the JNA withdrawal? If I could have 65 ter number 02067 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the international community in the shape of the UN Security Council was very anxious that all foreign forces leave BH in May 1992, and it passed two Resolutions in that connection.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We're looking at Resolution 752. Is that the first Resolution you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what demands did the Security Council put on the parties? The --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to answer that question, I would draw the Court's attention to numbered item 3, which would be on the next page or the following page in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly lower his microphones a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You heard that, Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They don't seem to have gone much lower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again calling the Court's attention to numbered paragraph 3 in the middle of the page, and number 4 and number 6. I won't read them since there are no translation issues and we can all see them, but number 3 refers to demanding that all forms of interference from outside BH, including units of the JNA, cease immediately. Paragraph 4 demands that those units of the Yugoslav People's Army and elements of the Croatian army now in BH must be withdrawn, et cetera. And paragraph 6 called upon all parties and others concerned to ensure that forcible expulsions, I guess that's not responsive to the question, but paragraphs 3 and 4 relate to the issue of foreign forces in BH.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 02067 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P201, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 02193 on the screen. Firstly at page 1 and then to page 3 of the English translation and pages 2 to 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, were the international community -- or Security Council satisfied with measures taken by the FRY to disengage itself from BiH in response to the previous Resolution we just saw?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In that regard, they issued a subsequent Resolution?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was that Resolution 757?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what demands did that -- did that take?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that connection I would call the Court's attention to the next page -- or page 3 of the Resolution beginning with numbered point 1 there in which we can see the Security Council condemns the failure of the authorities in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, including the Yugoslav People's Army, to take effective measures to fulfil the requirements of the previous Resolution that we'd just seen. And in point 3 it decided that all states shall adopt measures as set up below, which will apply until the Security Council decides that the authorities had taken effective measures. And in the points below it sets out certain measures restricting commerce between the FRY and other states.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P202, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell the Court what progress was made towards making peace after the sanctions were imposed.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the sanctions which were referred to were imposed, I don't believe the Resolution actually uses the word "sanctions," negotiations continued for a settlement in BH under the auspices of the international community. The so-called International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia was formed at the end of August or beginning of September 1992. The co-chairmen of that conference were Lord David Owen and Cyrus Vance, and the parties in conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina carried out negotiations throughout the autumn of 1992 under their auspices and began to come close to an agreement on a package of measures which came to be known as the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have Rule 65 ter number 06690 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, this is a transcript of the 20th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly session held on the 14th and 15th of September, 1992. What were the objectives of the Bosnian Serb leadership put forward in this Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if I could, first of all, ask the Registry to turn to page 51 of the English translation and 56 of the B/C/S simply so that we could see the speaker.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what did Radovan Karadzic have to say about -- about the objectives?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if I could -- sorry. If we can see, Your Honours, down at the bottom of the page president Radovan Karadzic begins to speak at that point. And it's at the top of the B/C/S page. If we could turn to page 55 of the English translation and page 60 of the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were the issues that -- that Mr. Karadzic was talking about here?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would call the Court's attention to the paragraph in the English beginning "Please," which -- in which it refers to the goals and issues in the negotiations. I will not read that whole paragraph, but just at the beginning: "Please, we know what our goals are. There can be some negotiations about the borders - a village here or there, that can be decided locally by whomever wants, but our goal is to protect our territory and endure long enough for all factors to agree." It then goes on to say "The factual situation will be decisive," and talks about the nature of the borders that he would like to see. He says: "We'll accept the external borders on the condition that we get the internal borders, but we will make do everything we can to make the internal borders thicker than the external borders without publicly saying so. Our borders towards the Muslims and Croats are to be thicker than our borders towards Serbia and Montenegro and the Serbian Krajina. That is why I ask you as deputies to never doubt what our goal is. Our goal is a state."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you can see the word "objective" is in the English translation that's on the screen, and Mr. Treanor uses the word "goal." I would ask that be admitted into evidence and marked for identification, and we will have a revised translation of that particular passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P203 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I rise just for a point clarification. When my colleague says we will have a revised translation, I take it what is going to occur is that the document will be sent to CLSS, and they will make a determination what the appropriate word is there, whether it's Mr. Treanor's word, or whether or not they stand by what they've already done. We just don't know at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note that that is a final CLSS translation at the moment. So as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it a final translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I guess the idea was that if it is a final translation, then we accept it as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. CLSS have in the past reviewed their final translations. They have gone back to rereview them if they are asked to do so, and in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If they are asked to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Our guideline here was that if it is the final CLSS, it is to be accepted as final, unless you are saying specifically that you are asking that we send it back for -- for review by CLSS. At this point in time, there is no such intention on the part of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- Mr. Treanor's evidence is on the record, so it can -- it can stay as is. It can be marked -- can it please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted into evidence. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I want to take you now to December 1992. What percentage of the territory did the Bosnian Serbs have in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If memory serves me correctly, I believe in the Bosnian Serb Assembly it was stated that in the autumn of 1992 that Bosnian Serb forces were in occupation of 70 per cent of the territory of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So by December 1992 were they -- were they willing to make peace at this point, the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They declared their willingness to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have Rule 65 ter number 09168 on the screen, please. It's a one-page document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Serbs issue any declaration to this effect?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did that occur?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 17th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what did they -- what did they pass? What did they issue?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They adopted a declaration proclaiming an end to the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is this the declaration that was passed at the 23rd Bosnian Serb Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the declaration I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What's the importance of this declaration in relation to borders?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that connection I would call the Court's attention to numbered paragraph 3, which states that: "Republika Srpska is ready to realise its borders as defined by its Assembly using political means. Its present boundaries are only temporary. The present boundaries of Republika Srpska are only temporary pending the conclusion of a peace agreement between the parties to the conflict in the former SR," that is socialist republic, "Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P204, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So we can see from that document that the Bosnian Serbs were willing to negotiate. Did the Belgrade leadership support this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have Rule 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- 06620 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In what way did the Belgrade leadership support it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could go to page 95 of the English and page 70 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is this document, Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is the stenographic notes of an enlarged session of the council for the reconciliation of the stands on state policies. This is a body that we encountered earlier in my testimony. I think we had at least one meeting in August of 1992 of this body. This is an enlarged session. Some people other than members of the council are present, including Serbian leaders from Croatia and Bosnia, such as Radovan Karadzic, and Momcilo Krajisnik, Nikola Koljevic, and many others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does that include also Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was there. And Zivota Panic is also there among the Belgrade leaders. In response to your first question, what did they do to encourage them, they pointed out to them that they had achieved their goals to an extent already that would warrant concluding peace and a peace which would confirm what they had gained already, and achieved the recognition, if you will, of the Bosnian Serb republic in BH.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can see on page 95 of the English translation and page 70 of the B/C/S that the speaker is Slobodan Milosevic. I can't see it on the English translation just yet. Can we go to the top of the page of the English translation. Could we go back one page, please. I'm sorry, on page 71 of the English translation. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what basically -- not basically. What -- what is Slobodan Milosevic saying in -- in this particular part of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it refers to the arguments that I mentioned before. I could read this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you could -- if you could try and summarise the facts so that we don't read in this quite lengthy slab.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Milosevic refers to the integrity of the Serbian people. He says: "We do de facto have that, because objectively and according to all our relations such as political, military, cultural, and educational we have that integrity." Then he goes on to say the important thing at this point is to get that recognised. And he states that a road which would lead to -- us to de jure recognition leads through a small labyrinth. We could never allow the change in a de facto situation, but through that small labyrinth, we would achieve sum things, if not in half a year, then in a year, if not an in a year, then two years. What do we gain? We gain that we would have fewer casualties, and in that way we would save our people." That was -- he's urging the conclusion of agreement in order to get recognition of what they have obtained already. He had it recognised de jure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Treanor, can I take you to page 96 of the English translation and page 95 of the B/C/S. Can you see there Radovan Karadzic is speaking?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is he saying in relation to the Neretva River?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He mentions the Neretva River in the context of some of the objections that he has to the status of the negotiations, as to the territories which would be granted to the Bosnian Serbs. If I could just read a bit of what Radovan Karadzic says. "Posavina and Podrinje are disputable." Posavina is the area along the Sava River, and Podrinje is the area along the Drina River in Bosnia. "Neretva is disputable, but we can live without Neretva. However, we cannot live without Podrinje and Posavina. Without them we have no chance of establishing the state and integrating in the future."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you just tell the Trial Chamber the importance of the Posavina corridor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we met the Posavina corridor before as the something -- corridor which would link the eastern and western halves of the Bosnian Serb republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I think in answer to Judge Moloto, the Presiding Judge, asked you whether --because you also, I think, mentioned Serbia in relation to your answer, not only was it linking the east and the west, but it was also linking the Serb-held -- the Bosnian Serb-held territory to Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would afford a link from large areas of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the western part of Republika Srpska to Serbia via the eastern half of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document, all those pages that I took Mr. Treanor to be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, that's page 71 and 96?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, of the English translation and 70 in -- no. 70, 95 and 96 of the B/C/S and 71 and 96 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those pages are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's pages would be Exhibit P205, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have Exhibit number 06673.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, were there any more discussions with the FRY leadership in January 1993 about the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 21st of January, 1993, there was another meeting of the same body.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 19 and 20 of the English translation and page 21 to 22 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was discussed in -- in this meeting? I'm sorry, again who was in attendance at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another enlarged session of that body, so people who were not members were also present, including Radovan Karadzic, Nikola Koljevic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Ratko Mladic, Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Treanor, what was discussed at this meeting in relation to the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they discussed further progress in the negotiations which had taken place between the two meetings we've been discussing, and the FRY leaders are again encouraging that an agreement be concluded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who is Mr. Vladislav Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic was at this time the Foreign Minister of Serbia. He had been the Foreign Minister of the FRY, and he would again become the Foreign Minister of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did he have to say at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this meeting in the passage we're looking at he pointed out another important aspect of the goals they were trying to achieve, not just territory per se, but as he says in the paragraph beginning with "Therefore," I'll just read a bit. "But what is more important is make the territory that we get nationally homogeneous as soon as possible but not by means of ethnic cleansings and so on. Ethnic cleansing are palm-offs. So we should use the peacetime process of the exchange of inhabitants, in other words migration and immigration which will flow. What is important is that life in future Bosnia becomes impossible and that everybody understands that individually -- understands that individually, that they rush off to their original provinces. This is a strategic goal to which we should aspire and which should be achieved."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I'm just reviewing my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, would you like the rest of the break to review your notes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that and come back at a quarter to. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 22 of the B/C/S and page 20 of the English translation of the document that we were just looking at before the break. Mr. Treanor, does Radovan Karadzic make any observations in relation to what Vladislav Jovanovic was talking about?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What does he say?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in response to an observation at the end of Mr. Jovanovic's speech suggesting that the process that he referred to could be achieved in -- as soon as in a couple of years' time, Dr. Karadzic replies: "In a year and two months if they would open the towns of Tuzla, Sarajevo, and Zenica," which are towns that had Serbian populations that were under the control of the BH government at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does he make any reference to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Further down he makes reference to the situation in Zvornik saying: "I think that this which Jovanovic is talking about has already happened to a huge extent. There was 50-50 of us in Zvornik. The number of inhabitants of Zvornik is now the same, approximately 50.000, and they are all Serbs. More than 24.000 Serbs from Zenica and Central Bosnia have arrived and stopped in Zvornik."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, pages 20 and 21 and 19 and 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Pages 19 and 20 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, 20 and 21 of the B/C/S and 19 and 20 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those pages are admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it may be a good idea if we could also have the first page of each of those documents so that at least you have some idea as to what document you're looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is true. Thank you so much. If we can do that. But now we've admitted so many of these documents without the first pages. I don't know whether the registrar will be able to identify them. From the beginning of Mr. Treanor's testimony, we've not been taking the first pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would be a matter of simply going to the documents which there are only single pages of -- of lengthy documents and then adding page 1 of each he have those documents where I haven't actually asked for the original page to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is correct. My question is I don't know whether the Registry will be able to do that without any help from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. We will -- we will provide them with the page numbers. We will review our notes and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Provide them with page numbers. I'm sorry if I was unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With my colleague's agreement, I would also suggest that we have in evidence with regard to the pages page 21, only because there is a continuation in terms of what Mr. Karadzic is saying. It's only part of what he's saying, and although they've commented on part of that part, at least we'll have the entire page -- the entire context of which that remark is made, which is one of the things I'd raised as a concern earlier on, and only because of the way the pages are broken up I suggest we also put in page 21.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May those pages be given an exhibit number, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So 65 ter number 06673 with English pages 19, 20, and 21 and B/C/S pages 20 and 21 will been admitted as P226, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the first pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the first pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Javier has brought to my attention that it's page 21 and 22 of the B/C/S, not pages 20 and 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, you hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. So pages 21 and 22 and page 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I want to move along three months to the beginning of April, 1993. Well, sorry, going back to the end of January. Between January and the beginning of April, how did the negotiations develop thereafter if you could very briefly explain to the Trial Chamber the position.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certain draft agreements were signed by various of the parties in -- to the conflict in BH. At the end of March, three documents were signed by representatives of the parties. All parties signed, all the documents except for the map, which was not signed by the Bosnian Serb party.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have Rule 65 ter number 02304.01 on the screen, please. And if I could have -- for the English it's the second translation that's attached to the e-court Rule 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, this is a transcript of a recording of the 26th Bosnian Serb Assembly session held in Belica on the 2nd of April, 1993. If we could go to page 8 of that document of the English translation and page 6 of the B/C/S. Did Mr. Karadzic in this Assembly session make reference to the amount of land that -- that the Bosnian Serbs possessed at that point?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They made reference to the amount of land which the Bosnian Serbs owned, in his opinion, and contrasted that with the amount of territory they would get according to the maps that had been offered them. In this -- I would call the Court's attention to that in this passage which is at the end of the second paragraph, the paragraph beginning with "First of all," at the end of -- toward the end of that paragraph he says that: "Although we possess 64 per cent of the land, and as a majority even after the genocide in the Second World War we live on 65 per cent of the territory, the former Bosnia-Herzegovina." When he says "possess" there, he's talking about ownership of the land. He's not talking about the military front lines at this point, but he believes that the Serbs own 64 per cent of the land and have inhabited 65 per cent and then goes on to say that according to the current map, it has been proposed that we live on just 43 per cent of the territory, which is pretty obvious that almost the entire Serbian population would voluntarily go to live in the areas where the Serbs have a majority. In other words, any Serbs living in the 57 per cent that was not given to the Bosnian Serbs would in his view have moved to the Serbian territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I think you had said earlier that by the end of December 1992, just prior to the declaration of the end of the war that was issued by the Bosnian Serbs, they had gained 70 per cent of the territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that's the figure that was given in the Bosnian Serb Assembly as far as the military control of land was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document be admitted into evidence, those pages at least, pages 1 and 8 of the English translation and pages 1 and 6 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They are so admitted. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Those pages will be Exhibit P207, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And around this time did the Security Council issue a further Resolution?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Around this time the Security Council, in fact, issued two more Resolutions in connection with the situation in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the reason for the issuing of the first Resolution? If I could have Rule 65 ter number 06568 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this Resolution the Security Council adduced a number of reasons for its action, beginning on the first page, reaffirming, and then in the second paragraph, taking note of a decision of the International Court of Justice in its order of 8 April 1993, calling on the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to immediately in pursuance of its undertaking on the convention of prevention of the crime of genocide of 9 December 1948 to take all measures within its power to prevent the commission of the crime of genocide. And then the Security Council went on to note features of the situation on the ground in BH which gave a concern at this point, in particular the situation around the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was reference also made to the FRY and the supply of material to the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Among the demands of the Security Council was one that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and this is in the next page of the English under point 3, the security counsel "Demands that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia immediately cease the supply of military arms, equipment, and services to the Bosnian Serb paramilitary units in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With respect to the reference to paramilitary organs -- units, I'm sorry, the -- were the Bosnian Serb forces recognised by the United Nations Security Council?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that the Bosnians -- the Security Council recognised anybody beyond Member States. They referred to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If -- and I believe the witness has now answered the question with regard to the specific matter asked by the Prosecution if the Security Council did not recognise anything other than Member States, and now it goes beyond the purview of his knowledge as to what the Security Council did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question has been answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry. I will -- can I have a moment, Your Honour. Your Honour, what's the objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection was just that the witness was going beyond the purview of both his expertise and the question by trying to explain further, having said that the United Nations recognises Member States only and nothing beyond.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor may be in a position to answer the question as to whether the United Nations Security Council does or does not recognise entities as opposed to Member States. I'm sure Mr. Treanor can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But he has answered that. He said to you that the United Nations recognises Member States only, and he's not aware of anything beyond that that they recognise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I was going -- I understood the question. I was going to move on, but I wondered what the objection was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection was stopping him from going beyond the answer having given the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But Mr. Guy-Smith rose after he'd answered the question, so I was at a loss to know what the issue was once the question had been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The issue was once the question had been answered the witness was carrying on to comment on things that were not part of the answer -- part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Mr. Treanor, if the United Nations Security Council does not recognise entities, then similarly they would not recognise an army to that entity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question, Your Honour. Could I have that document admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P208, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did the United Nations Security Council impose any sanctions on the FRY and, if so, why?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 06623 on the screen please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time the Security Council threatened to take additional measures restricting commerce with the FRY under certain conditions which, in fact, were fulfilled. In that connection I could direct the Court's attention to page 3 of the English version of the Resolution. Paragraph number 10 in which the Security Council decides that the provisions set forth in paragraphs 12 to 30 below shall, to the extent that they establish obligations beyond those establish by its earlier relevant Resolutions, come into force nine days after the date of the adoption of the present Resolution, unless the Security General has reported to the Council that the Bosnian Serb party has joined the other parties in signing the peace plan and in implementing it and that the Bosnian Serbs have ceased their military attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I suppose then, Mr. Treanor, the record says you said, "unless the Security General," did you mean Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secretary-General.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did the -- what date was this Security Council Resolution?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Resolution was adopted on the 17th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the previous Resolution that we saw, Exhibit P208, do you recall the date of that Resolution?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was adopted on the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So with respect to the Resolution adopted on the 17th of April, did the Security Council then set out the sanctions which would come into effect nine days after the adoption of the present Resolution?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are set out further below, and reference is made to paragraphs 12 to 30 below which contain restrictions against commerce with the, as it puts it, the United Nations Protected Areas in the Republic of Croatia in those areas of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina under control the Bosnian Serb forces, and then beginning in paragraph 13 makes reference to restrictions on the -- in relation to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can that document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P209, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did the Bosnian Serbs react to this Resolution, the one of the 17th of April? If could I have Rule 65 ter number 06750 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not sign the peace plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did the Belgrade leadership correspond in any way with the Bosnian Serbs in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The document we have on the screen at the moment is the minutes of the 29th Bosnian Serb Assembly session held on the 25th and 26th of April in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who else was present besides the Bosnian Serbs? Did -- was anyone from Belgrade present?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and during the course of the session Vladislav Jovanovic arrived. He was at this time again the Foreign Minister of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of him being at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He brought with him a letter from Dobrica Cosic, Slobodan Milosevic, and Momir Bulatovic encouraging the Bosnian Serbs to accept the peace plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what was the position taken by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly, in response to the letter, expressing its surprise did two things. It took a vote on the plan which, according to the minutes of the meeting --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 of the --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be on the next page of the English yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Page 2 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Toward the bottom of that page. Now the middle. A short paragraph is there, and I would draw the Court's attention to that. It simply notes that all 73 deputies present voted against accepting the Vance-Owen maps. Then the second thing the Assembly did is described at the bottom of the page where they -- it's mentioned that they adopted a decision to hold a referendum in the RS on specifically that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that document be admitted into evidence, pages 1, 2, and 3 of the English translation and page 1 and 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those pages are admitted. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P210, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the whole document is only three pages in B/C/S and in English, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you've given us three pages in English already.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. So for completeness, can the whole document of the B/C/S be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, will you please do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
